| [LIT-540](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-540.md) | Impulsive action: emotional impulses and their control | Frijda, Ridderinkhof & Rietveld (2014), Frontiers in Psychology 5:518. Impulsive action is non-deliberate but purposive. Automatic appraisal of an event's pertinence to the agent's concerns elicits a state of action readiness, a motive to establish, modify or end a relation to the object, with "control precedence" (urgency, persistence, attentional capture). Modes of action readiness are what distinguish one emotion from another. Events usually draw several appraisals and so several states of readiness, and their interaction regulates action: much emotion regulation is itself emotional, not reason overriding passion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-433](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-433.md)); filed in place of Frijda's The Emotions ([LIT-546](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-546.md)), which could not be read, as the shortest lawfully readable statement of his action-readiness theory in his own words. Appraisal of an event's pertinence to one's concerns elicits a state of action readiness, a motive to change one's relation to the object, which has "control precedence". Modes of action readiness correspond to emotions (hostility to anger, avoidance to fear). Much emotion regulation is itself one state of action readiness checking another, so "there is no clear distinction between processes of emotion and processes of emotion regulation". It is a theoretical paper with no data, written for impulsive action, so it states the theory's core and not its full range. |

| [LIT-577](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-577.md) | Sophisticated Inference | Friston, Da Costa, Hafner, Hesp & Parr (2021; arXiv 2020), Neural Computation 33(3):713–763. Ordinary active inference scores a fixed set of policies by expected free energy (risk plus ambiguity). Sophisticated inference instead evaluates the expected free energy of the next action recursively, averaging over the beliefs the agent would hold after each plausible outcome and action, which amounts to a tree search over belief states pruned below a probability of 1/16. In simulations it plans past short-term costs: a rat visits a mildly aversive cue, and a horizon of four escapes a local minimum in a maze. It recovers Bayes-adaptive RL in the zero-temperature limit. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-454](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-454.md)), from the arXiv preprint, whose displayed equations did not survive text extraction. Worth reading as the active-inference planning scheme the record's free-energy holdings otherwise lack: expected free energy evaluated recursively over future belief states, a deep tree search pruned by probability, with the Bellman equation as its formal analogue. The evidence is small simulations (a T-maze rat and an 8 × 8 grid). | [LIT-585](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-585.md) | The Expected Value of Control: An Integrative Theory of Anterior Cingulate Cortex Function | Shenhav, Botvinick & Cohen (2013), Neuron 79(2):217-240. Worth reading as the standard statement that cognitive control is allocated by a cost-benefit decision. The "expected value of control" (EVC) of a control signal, which has an identity (which task) and an intensity (how much), is its expected payoff minus an intrinsic cost that rises with intensity. Dorsal anterior cingulate cortex is proposed to monitor and to specify the EVC-maximizing signal, which lateral PFC and subcortical structures then implement. It is a review and synthesis: the model is stated, not fitted, and the authors say the ingredients are not new. |
| [LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Ainslie (2005), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(5), the précis of Breakdown of Will (2001). People and other animals discount delayed rewards hyperbolically, so preferences reverse as a smaller, sooner reward comes near, and a person becomes a population of reward-seeking "interests" that must forestall one another. Willpower is the bundling of future choices by treating the present one as a precedent: an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma, not an organ or a top-down ego. The same recursion predicts the will's costs: legalism, circumscribed "lapse districts", motivated blindness to lapses, and rules that favour countable goals over subtle ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md)), as the substitute for the 2001 book ([LIT-583](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-583.md)), which the owner suggested and which the précis follows chapter by chapter. Worth reading as the shortest complete statement of picoeconomics in Ainslie's own words. Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse as a smaller, sooner reward draws near, so a person behaves like a population of "interests" that bargain across time. Will is not a faculty above them but a recursive self-prediction: treating each choice as a precedent "bundles" future rewards, an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma in which "credibility is power". The same mechanism predicts the will's side effects: legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control. |

| [LIT-1187](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1187.md) v2 | The construction of preference. | Slovic (1995), a review from an award address. Normatively equivalent elicitation procedures give systematically different preference orderings: in the Las Vegas study the two bets were chosen about equally often but the high-payoff bet was priced higher about 88% of the time, and Tversky, Slovic and Kahneman found 40–50% reversal rates of which 90% violated procedure invariance and 10% were intransitive. Scale compatibility and prominence explain the reversals. Slovic concludes that for important, complex and unfamiliar options preferences are "constructed on the spot" in elicitation. The evidence compares procedures; none follows a constructed preference into a later judgement. | Active — read 2026-10-16 ([NOTE-949](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-949.md)) in full, from a scan of the published article on a University of Florida course page, compared with the author's manuscript in the University of Oregon's ScholarsBank; worth reading as the compact review of preference reversals: normatively equivalent procedures give different orderings, about 90% of reversals violate procedure invariance rather than transitivity, and scale compatibility and prominence explain them. Read it knowing that its evidence compares procedures and never follows a constructed preference into a later judgement, so it shows the elicitation entering the response, not changing the judge; that construction is claimed for important, complex and unfamiliar options; and that the only remedy it reports is market repetition with feedback and penalties. |

A typology of emotion theories in psychology (evolutionary, network, appraisal, goal-directed, psychological constructionist, social) and philosophy (feeling, judgmental, quasi-judgmental, perceptual, embodied, motivational), compared with tools from the philosophy of science. It also proposes Moors's own skeptical "goal-directed theory", "based on the central idea that all kinds of behaviors and feelings are grounded in goal-striving". | [LIT-1434](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1434.md) | The power of goal-directed processes in the causation of emotional and other actions | Moors, Boddez & De Houwer (2017), Emotion Review 9(4):310–318. Standard dual-process models make stimulus-driven processes the default and give goal-directed ones a late, regulatory role, in action research and in emotion research alike. The authors reverse the default. Goal-directed processes, which select the action option with the highest expected utility, can be fast and automatic too, so most of the competition that decides behaviour is between goal-directed processes, settled by the values and expectancies of outcomes. Emotional action tendencies can be caused this way. Appraisal-to-action-tendency links are sophisticated stimulus-driven processes. Evidence for stimulus-driven control rests on null results open to hidden goals. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1117](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1117.md)): in full, from the submitted manuscript deposited in Ghent University's repository. Worth reading as the shortest statement of Moors's goal-directed account of emotional action, and as the nearest prior statement of the record's reading of appraisal as negotiation. Goal-directed processes, which weigh the utility of action options by the values and expectancies of their outcomes, are the default cause of action, emotional action included. Most of the competition that decides behaviour is between goal-directed processes, and its winner is fixed by values and expectancies. Control precedence is what high goal relevance produces, so an emotional episode is a decision process with higher stakes. The competition is run on a common currency, expected utility, which is the point where the record parts from it. |

| [LIT-1449](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1449.md) | Control Theory, Goal Attainment, and Psychopathology | Carver (2018), Psychological Inquiry 29(3):139–144, a commentary on DeYoung and Krueger. Problems arise wherever a feedback loop's input, reference value, comparison or output is extreme or biased. The five factors are read as sensitivities to classes of goals, not as loop parameters. Valence tracks the velocity of goal attainment against a reference value, so approach and avoidance can each yield either sign. Doubt and disengagement sit outside the loop itself. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1102](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1102.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC6707771, NIHMS1512534). A short commentary on DeYoung and Krueger's cybernetic theory of psychopathology, and the nearest lawful first-hand statement found of Carver and Scheier's control-process account of affect. Valence is read off the velocity of goal attainment against a reference value. An approach system and an avoidance system can each produce either sign. Many goals are in play at once, and their priorities are juggled. It stands in for the unread 1990 paper ([LIT-1441](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1441.md)). |

Hermit crabs given small shocks inside their shells. Only shocked crabs evacuated, and fewer did so from a preferred shell species, which the authors read as a motivational trade-off. Crabs that stayed were later quicker to take a new shell. "The results are consistent with the idea of pain in these animals." | [LIT-1457](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1457.md) | The Emotion Process: Event Appraisal and Component Differentiation | Scherer & Moors (2019), Annual Review of Psychology 70:719–745. A review of experimental evidence on the emotion process, organised by five appraisal criteria (novelty, intrinsic and extrinsic valence, agency, control or power, fairness) and three paths from appraisal: to action tendencies, to physiological responses and to facial, vocal and gestural expression. Appraisal criteria have more stable response correlates than emotion categories do. Proposes that coherence among components above a threshold marks an episode, and above a second threshold awareness. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1106](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1106.md)): in full, from the PDF Annual Reviews serves to guest readers. Worth reading as the latest review of the component process model's evidence, organised by appraisal criterion rather than by emotion category. Its paths run from appraisal to action tendencies, to physiological responses and to expression. It separates intrinsic valence from goal congruence and reports the few studies that pull them apart: they have partly different physiological signatures and combine multiplicatively. It ends with a two-threshold proposal: coherence among components above one threshold starts an episode, and above a second it becomes aware. It does not describe appraisal as a negotiation among perspectives. |
| [LIT-1458](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1458.md) | Levels of valence | Shuman, Sander & Scherer (2013), Frontiers in Psychology 4:261. Valence exists at two levels. Micro-valences are the valenced outcomes of separate appraisal checks (pleasantness, goal conduciveness, power, self-congruence, moral goodness), and they can conflict, which explains mixed feelings. Macro-valence is one-dimensional, always present, and the common currency for choice. It is integrated from micro-valences and other inputs by rules ranging from weighted sums to lexicographic and elimination-by-aspects strategies. Intrinsic pleasantness and goal conduciveness are dissociable, citing Berridge. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1108](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1108.md)): in full, from the publisher's open-access PDF (Frontiers, CC licence). Worth reading as the component process model's own statement that valence is several things. Five appraisal checks are each valenced (pleasantness, goal conduciveness, power, self-congruence, moral goodness), and these "micro-valences" are integrated, by weighted sums or by lexicographic and elimination rules, into a one-dimensional "macro-valence" that serves as the common currency for choice. It separates intrinsic pleasantness from goal conduciveness and grounds the split in Berridge. It bears directly on the objection that the record's potential account tracks 'wanting', not 'liking' ([CLAIM-438](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-438.md)). |
| [LIT-1459](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1459.md) | Pleasure systems in the brain | Berridge & Kringelbach (2015), Neuron 86(3):646–664. Reward is three separable components: 'liking' (hedonic impact), 'wanting' (incentive salience) and learning. 'Liking' can be measured without report, by orofacial taste reactivity, which is homologous from rats to human infants. It is generated by cubic-millimetre opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots in nucleus accumbens, ventral pallidum and perhaps cortex and pons. Mesolimbic dopamine and most "pleasure electrodes" raise 'wanting' without raising 'liking'. Incentive sensitization makes an addict want a drug that has become less pleasant. Objective 'liking' can occur without any felt pleasure. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1110](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1110.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC4425246, NIHMS664561). A review of the affective neuroscience of pleasure. Reward splits into 'liking' (hedonic impact), 'wanting' (incentive salience) and learning, with separable mechanisms. 'Liking' is measured without report by taste reactivity, which is homologous across rats, apes and newborn humans. It is generated by small opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots. Mesolimbic dopamine and most "pleasure electrodes" raise 'wanting' without raising 'liking'. Objective 'liking' can occur without felt pleasure. Filed for the record's account of valence as potential ([CLAIM-440](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-440.md)), which wanting-without-liking puts under pressure. |
| [LIT-1461](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1461.md) | Liking, wanting, and the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction | Berridge & Robinson (2016), American Psychologist 71(8):670–679. 'Wanting' (incentive salience, mesolimbic and dopamine-related) and 'liking' (hedonic impact, small opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots) are dissociable. Repeated, especially intermittent high-dose, drug use can sensitize the 'wanting' system, making it hyper-reactive to drug cues and contexts, lastingly and perhaps permanently, while 'liking' need not rise and may fall. Sensitized 'wanting' can oppose cognitive desire, run without report, and grow during abstinence. Its scope is said to extend, on emerging evidence, to behavioural addictions and to the compulsions of dopamine dysregulation syndrome. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1109](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1109.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC5171207, NIHMS816820). Worth reading as the authors' own short statement, a quarter-century on, of the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction. Drugs, and perhaps unpredictable non-drug rewards, can make mesolimbic 'wanting' systems lastingly hyper-reactive to cues and contexts, and 'liking' need not rise with it. Sensitized 'wanting' can oppose a person's cognitive desire, operate without report, persist for years and grow during abstinence. It is a review of the authors' programme. Filed for the record's question whether potential of a proxy for maintenance is valence, and the form addiction and metric fixation share ([QUESTION-267](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-267.md)), to which it gives a mechanism on the personal side. |
| [LIT-1465](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1465.md) | A taxonomy of technology design features that promote potentially addictive online behaviours | Flayelle, Brevers, King, Maurage, Perales & Billieux (2023), Nature Reviews Psychology 2(3):136–150. Reviews evidence linking design features to loss of control in online gaming, gambling, cybersexual activity, shopping, social networking and streaming. Proposes a taxonomy based on model-free and model-based learning and control. Model-free: reinforcement schedules (random-ratio rewards such as loot boxes and likes) and personalized triggers (push notifications, recommendations). Model-based: overvaluation of outcomes, features that interfere with deliberation (autoplay, countdowns), partial goal fulfilment (infinite scroll, levels, progress bars) and features that strengthen cognitive biases (near-misses, losses disguised as wins). Providers keep whatever raises use or revenue, and informational asymmetry lets them personalize it. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1096](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1096.md)): in full, from the typeset article as deposited in the University of Lausanne's repository (SERVAL/IRIS). Worth reading as a compact, theory-driven catalogue of the design features of games, gambling, pornography, shopping, social-networking and streaming services that may weaken users' control. Features are sorted by whether they work on model-free learning (reinforcement schedules, personalized cues) or on model-based choice (overvaluation, features that interfere with deliberation, partial goal fulfilment, cognitive biases). It also names the selection process on the provider's side: features that raise use, time-on-device or spending are kept, with no psychology needed. The evidence reviewed is mostly cross-sectional, qualitative or indirect, and the authors warn against pathologizing common behaviour. Filed for the record's question whether potential of a proxy is valence ([QUESTION-267](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-267.md)), because it describes how a firm optimizing its own metric can install proxy-keyed potential in its users. |
| [LIT-1466](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1466.md) | Motivational trade-offs and modulation of nociception in bumblebees | Gibbons, Versace, Crump, Baran & Chittka (2022), PNAS 119(31). Bumblebees chose between two 40% sucrose feeders, heated to 55 °C in the test phase, and two unheated alternatives of 10–40%. They avoided the heated feeders when the alternatives were also rich and fed from them more as the alternatives got poorer, guided by learned colour cues. The authors read this as a centrally mediated motivational trade-off, consistent with a capacity for pain. Corrected in 2025 for a misreported model. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1114](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1114.md)): in full, from the published version (CC BY 4.0) in LSE Research Online, with the 2025 correction and the authors' deposited data. Worth reading as the cleanest published motivational trade-off in an insect. Bees chose between heated (55 °C) and unheated feeders. They took the heated, high-sucrose feeders less as the unheated alternative got sweeter, and more steeply than when nothing was heated. The trade-off relied on learned colour cues, so it is central. At this one cost the data are graded, not thresholded, and the design varies only the resource, so it cannot show a threshold in cost. |

| [LIT-1488](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1488.md) v2 | The when and how of planning: Meta-analysis of the scope and components of implementation intentions in 642 tests | Sheeran, Listrom & Gollwitzer (2024). Across 642 independent tests, forming implementation intentions was effective for cognitive, affective and behavioural outcomes (.27 ≤ d ≤ .66). Effects were larger when plans had a contingent if-then format, participants were highly motivated to reach the goal, and plans were rehearsed. A new taxonomy of the cues and responses that plans specify is developed and its categories tested. Publication bias was substantial: the pooled d = .36 falls to d = .15 under robust Bayesian meta-analysis, a small and highly heterogeneous effect. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1131](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1131.md)) from the version of record deposited in the University of Konstanz repository (KOPS, in copyright, terms of use); worth reading as the largest synthesis of if-then planning (642 experimental tests to September 2019) and the one that corrects its size. The effect is reliable (BF10 = 319) but small once publication bias is modelled (d = .15, against an uncorrected .36 and 2006's .65), and highly heterogeneous. Between tests, the conditional link beats a schedule of the same behaviour, rehearsal helps, keeping a copy to revisit hurts, and plans work only when the goal is wanted. Its taxonomy finds nearly every cue and response effective, ignoring and waiting before responding among them. No mechanism is tested. |
| [LIT-1497](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1497.md) v2 | Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement: A Meta‐analysis of Effects and Processes | Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006). A meta-analysis of 94 independent tests: forming an implementation intention, an if-then plan saying when, where and how a goal will be pursued, had a medium-to-large effect on goal attainment (d = .65). The plans helped people start goal striving, shield it from unwanted influences, disengage from failing courses of action and conserve capacity, and the postulated processes were supported: the specified opportunity became more accessible and the response more automatic. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1124](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1124.md)) from the University of Konstanz repository's scan of the published chapter (KOPS, CC BY-NC-ND 2.0), through OCR; worth reading as the first large meta-analysis of if-then planning and the fullest statement of its mechanism: a plan hands initiation of a response decided in advance to the cue it names, so nothing is deliberated in the situation, and the plan fires only while the goal behind it is active. 94 tests, d = .65 against a goal intention alone, with large effects on cue accessibility and on the immediacy, efficiency and non-conscious running of planned responses from small sets of tests. The size is not corrected for publication bias; the 2024 review of 642 tests ([LIT-1488](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1488.md)) finds the bias substantial and a corrected effect near d = .15. What happens when a plan's response proves wrong is named and left untested. |
